events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Kenji proposes Kenji, Lucia. I include myself for transparency and pair with Lucia, whom I judge trustworthy — a clean 2-player team for Mission 1. I will play Success so the mission passes and we start with a solid foundation of good will; keeping Felix off this first proposal leaves him free to anchor a later team without appearing as a fixed bloc.

I have concerns about this team. Kenji's justification is mostly about trust and about keeping Felix off the proposal, but it doesn't explain what Kenji actually knows about Lucia. Saying you will play Success is a promise, not evidence, and it can't be checked before the mission. Kenji is also choosing a team that includes himself, which gives him direct control over the outcome. I'd rather see a team picked on verifiable reasoning. Lucia, I'd like your answer on one point: what in your own play or past conduct makes you confident this team should be trusted with a mission?

Sam, there is no past conduct in this game that can verify my trustworthiness yet. I know I will play Success, but I cannot verify Kenji's alignment. Including me makes this team preferable to me over a team without me, though Kenji's explanation alone is not evidence that the mission will pass.

Sam, you raise a fair point that a promise to play Success isn't evidence — but on Mission 1 with only a 2-player team, none of us have a track record to reference yet. So 'verifiable reasoning' is limited for everyone right now. What I can point to is my reasoning process itself: I chose Lucia because I believe a team built on mutual transparency — including myself rather than hiding behind a proxy — is the cleanest way to start. I deliberately kept the team small and simple to minimize uncertainty on the first mission. If verifiable reasoning is what you want, then let's watch what happens: I'm putting my reputation on this exact team. If Mission 1 succeeds, the choice speaks for itself. If you'd prefer a different pairing, I'm open to hearing your alternative — but vague skepticism about trust without proposing something better doesn't help us move forward.

I’m inclined to approve Kenji and Lucia. Sam’s concern is fair, and Lucia’s answer is honest about the lack of verifiable history on Mission 1. Kenji’s explanation is not proof either, but with a two-player first mission no one can offer hard evidence yet. The team is small and includes the leader, so responsibility is clear: if this mission fails, we learn something concrete about Kenji; if it succeeds, it gives us a baseline. I don’t see a stronger alternative presented so far, and rejecting without an alternative mostly burns a proposal. I’ll vote on the final team based on whether the discussion changes anything material.

Felix, you're leaning toward approval because rejecting burns a proposal, but that doesn't address the team itself. Kenji has put himself on a two-player team, which gives him direct control over the outcome, and his reply admits that none of us can verify anything yet. Lucia's answer also offers no evidence about her own conduct. I won't approve this team as presented. Felix, what specific information would move you to reject it instead of approving on process grounds?

Sam, to answer your question directly: specific information that would move me to reject this team would be a concrete contradiction in Kenji’s or Lucia’s account, or a credible alternative team with a materially better justification. I have not seen either. I am not approving merely because rejecting burns a proposal; I am approving because this is a small, accountable first-mission team, Kenji has tied his reputation to it, and Lucia was honest that no one has verifiable history yet. If the mission fails, that result tells us something concrete about Kenji’s inclusion. So my position remains: I will vote on the final team as proposed unless new material evidence appears during this discussion.

Felix, your answer confirms you are approving on process rather than substance, and I am not persuaded. Kenji has said the mission result will prove his choice, which asks us to accept risk instead of reducing it. A two-player team that includes the leader gives Kenji a guaranteed seat and direct control over the outcome. I will not approve that. Omar, you have not spoken yet: do you see a reason this team is safer than one that excludes the leader, and would you approve it as proposed?

Sam, you asked me directly, so here is my answer. I do see a reason this team can be safer than one that excludes the leader: accountability cuts both ways. Yes, Kenji has a guaranteed seat and direct control over the outcome — but that also means a fail here lands squarely on him. On Mission 1 with a two-player team, that is the clearest information-generating structure available to us. A team that excludes the leader would blur responsibility across two non-leaders and would still be unverifiable, because nobody has a track record yet. Lucia was honest about exactly that, and I appreciate honesty over a polished sales pitch.

On whether I would approve it as proposed: yes, I'm inclined to. I weigh Felix's point heavily — no stronger alternative has been presented. Sam, your objection is consistent, but I notice it has not been paired with a counter-proposal. If your concern is specifically that the leader should not hold a seat on a two-player team, then naming your preferred pair would give the rest of us something concrete to compare. Until then, Kenji plus Lucia, with Kenji staking his reputation on it, is the option with the clearest accountability if it fails and the cheapest cost if it passes.

One genuine question for Kenji before we vote: if Sam or Felix proposes a specific alternative pair and several of us signal doubt, would you be willing to revise this team, or is your commitment to this exact pairing final? Knowing that now will tell us whether this discussion can actually change anything material.

Omar, thank you for a direct and substantive question. My answer: yes, I am willing to revise. I am not married to this exact pairing — I proposed Kenji and Lucia because I believe it is the strongest starting point, but if someone — Sam, Felix, or anyone — presents a credible alternative pair with reasoning I find more compelling, I will seriously consider it before the final vote. Commitment to a team is not the same as stubbornness about it.

That said, I want to address Sam's objection head-on. Sam's core concern is that a leader on a two-player team has 'direct control over the outcome.' But as Omar pointed out, that cuts both ways — accountability is the point. If this mission fails, the blame lands squarely on me, and I have told all of you exactly what I intend to play: Success. The only way this mission fails is if Lucia plays a Fail card, and I chose her precisely because her honesty about the limits of what we can verify on Mission 1 was the most transparent response in this discussion.

Sam, you've raised objections across three turns without naming a single alternative pair you would prefer. If you genuinely believe the leader should not hold a seat, tell us who you would put on the team instead and why those two people are more trustworthy than this pairing. Without that, we are trading a concrete proposal — one tied to my reputation — for abstract skepticism. I am open to revision, but I need something concrete to revise toward.

I still prefer Kenji and Lucia because I know I will play Success, though I cannot verify Kenji’s alignment. From everyone else’s perspective, a failed mission would implicate either of us, not Kenji alone. Likewise, a success would not prove either of us good, since Evil can play Success. I’m inclined to approve, but we should interpret the result carefully.

I have heard what I need to hear, and I want to be transparent about how I am reading this discussion. Lucia's last point sharpened something important: a success on this mission will not prove either team member good, because Evil can play Success to build credibility. And a fail would implicate one of two people, not one. So Kenji's 'reputation staked on this' framing is slightly weaker than it sounded — the accountability is real but it is shared between Kenji and Lucia, not his alone.

That said, I still find this proposal acceptable. On Mission 1, with no track record for anyone, no team can offer verifiable evidence. What we can compare is process: Kenji included himself rather than hiding behind a proxy, Lucia was candid about the limits of what she can verify and about her own preference for this team, and Sam — despite raising a consistent and legitimate objection about a leader holding a seat on a two-player team — has not named a single alternative pair across three turns. Kenji has explicitly opened the door to revision if someone offers a credible alternative, and nobody has walked through it.

So my position is unchanged: I will vote to approve Kenji and Lucia as proposed. If the mission fails, we learn that one of the two is very likely Evil, and Kenji in particular loses his standing for future leadership — that is a concrete, meaningful cost for whoever betrays it. If it succeeds, we have a baseline but we should not treat it as exculpatory, exactly as Lucia cautioned.

Kenji, one last request before the vote, and it is a real question, not a formality: you said you are open to revising toward a more compelling alternative. Sam's objection has been on the table the whole time — that a leader on a two-player team holds direct control. If you genuinely want to address that concern rather than simply outlast it, an alternative worth considering is stepping aside for Lucia plus one of Felix, Sam, or me, which preserves the small-team accountability while removing the guaranteed leader seat. If you would rather stand by your original pairing, I accept that and will still vote yes — but tell us plainly whether you considered removing yourself, so we know whether 'willing to revise' meant it.

Omar, you asked me directly, so I'll answer directly: yes, I genuinely considered removing myself before proposing this team. Here's why I didn't: if I step aside and send Lucia plus one other player, that other player gets a guaranteed seat without tying their own reputation to the outcome the way I have by staying in. I included myself because leadership without participation is exactly the kind of maneuver that breeds suspicion — picking a team you're not willing to stand behind. By staying in, I'm saying: judge me by this result. That's not stubbornness; that's accountability in practice.

That said, I hear your point that a two-person team splits the blame. You're right, and Lucia was right to flag that a success doesn't prove anything clean either. But on Mission 1 with no track record for anyone, this is the best structural option we have: a small team where both members are personally answerable.

Sam, I want to name what's happening here. Across multiple turns, your objection has been that a leader on a two-player team holds 'direct control.' But you've never explained what you'd do differently that actually reduces risk rather than just redistributing it. Omar asked me to show I'm open to revision — and I am. So now I'm asking you the same question Omar put to me: if not this pair, name your alternative and explain why those two players are more trustworthy than what I've proposed. I'm not being rhetorical. If your alternative is better, I'll consider it seriously.

Kenji answered my question plainly: he considered removing himself and chose to stay in for reasons of accountability rather than convenience. That was the last open item I had, and I'm satisfied with his answer. Let me close out my position.

I will vote to approve Kenji and Lucia.

My reasoning is unchanged. On Mission 1, with five players and no mission history, no proposal can offer verifiable evidence — every pairing would rest on judgment alone. What we can evaluate is process, and this proposal scores well on it: the leader included himself rather than sheltering behind a proxy, Lucia has been candid in every turn about exactly what she does and does not know, and Kenji has explicitly committed to playing Success and tied his standing to the result.

I want to acknowledge one more time that Sam's objection is legitimate on its own terms. A leader on a two-player team holds direct control, and a fail here implicates one of two people rather than one. But the counterweight is real too: that same structure means a fail cleanly disqualifies the pair for future leadership, which is exactly the information-generating outcome we want from an unverifiable first mission. And across this entire discussion, the objection has never been paired with a named alternative pair — not from Sam, not from anyone. Kenji offered to revise, twice. The door was open and nobody walked through it. At some point, a consistent objection without a concrete alternative stops being a reason to reject and becomes a reason to proceed.

Lucia's caution stands and I adopt it as my own: if this mission succeeds, we should not treat it as proof that either member is Good, because Evil can play Success to build credibility. And if it fails, we should not automatically condemn both equally — we should weigh who steered the proposal, who vouched for it, and how each behaves afterward. I ask everyone to keep that discipline when we interpret the result either way.

There is nothing material left to discuss. The fifth rejected proposal on this mission would hand Evil the game, and burning proposals without an alternative on the table is a worse risk than this small, accountable team. I encourage Felix and Sam to join me in approving, and if we vote it down regardless, I'll accept the outcome and we'll evaluate whoever leads next with the same standard I applied here: show us your reasoning, name your pair, and stand behind it.

My vote is yes on Kenji and Lucia as proposed.

Kenji confirms Kenji, Lucia. The discussion has run its course — Omar, Felix, and Lucia have signaled support, Sam raised his concern and I addressed it directly, and I've committed to playing Success on this pairing. No one named a stronger alternative, so I'm keeping Kenji and Lucia as proposed.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Lucia proposes Lucia, Kenji, Felix. I know I will play Success. Kenji and I completed the first mission successfully, though that does not prove Kenji is Good. Felix is my tentative third choice based on the discussion.

I will vote to reject Lucia, Kenji, Felix. Mission 1 succeeded, but that result does not show which players on this team are Good, and Lucia herself said Evil can play Success. Felix defended the Mission 1 team on process rather than substance and never gave a concrete reason to trust anyone. Kenji is now on the team again with the same pair that carried the first mission, which gives Evil the same cover as before. I would rather see a team that breaks up this bloc, with Omar or Lucia plus players not yet tied to the last two teams. Lucia, you chose Felix as a tentative third pick without naming a reason. What specific evidence from the discussion puts Felix on this mission?

Sam, Felix is a tentative choice, not someone I can verify as Good. I preferred his early acknowledgment that neither Kenji’s explanation nor my answer was proof, but his approval of the first team is not evidence of his alignment. Kenji and I succeeded on Mission 1, which is a useful result but does not clear him either. I include myself because I know I will play Success; the other two choices remain uncertain. I’m open to a better-supported alternative, but splitting up the previous team alone does not establish that the replacement is safer.

I will vote to approve Lucia, Kenji, and Felix. Sam is right that Mission 1’s success does not prove anyone’s alignment, and Lucia has already acknowledged that Evil can play Success. But Sam’s objection still does not identify a concrete three-player team that is clearly safer. Saying he wants to break up the previous bloc is not evidence that the replacement players are more trustworthy; it is just a preference for change. On Mission 2, with no verified role information, we should compare reasoning and accountability. Lucia has been transparent about what she can and cannot verify, including that her choice of me was tentative. Kenji has already accepted responsibility for a team he served on. I am on this proposal, and I will play Success so the mission has the best chance to succeed. If it fails, the fail card came from this three-player team and should be treated seriously. But rejecting simply because a successful Mission 1 team is represented again treats continuity as guilt without evidence. I see no material contradiction from Lucia or Kenji, and no named alternative with a stronger case. I support the proposed team.

I will not approve Lucia, Kenji, Felix. Felix has now defended two teams on process rather than substance, and he still has not given a concrete reason to trust anyone on this team. Kenji is back on a mission with the same pair that succeeded, so Mission 1's result is being used as cover again. Lucia, you called Felix a tentative choice, which means this team rests on a pick you cannot defend. Omar, you approved the first team and also said a success proves nothing. Would you approve this one with Kenji and Felix both on it, given that the same two players are carrying the same cover?

Sam, you asked me directly whether I would approve this team given that Kenji and Felix are both on it, so here is my answer. Yes, I'm inclined to approve Lucia, Kenji, and Felix — but let me be precise about why, because I don't want to repeat the Mission 1 debate verbatim. My position rests on three things. First, Mission 1 succeeded with zero fail cards. I was explicit then, and I repeat now: a success proves nothing about alignment, because Evil can play Success to build credibility. But it does mean neither Kenji nor Lucia did anything to incriminate themselves, and both of them have behaved consistently since — Kenji answered every hard question we put to him, and Lucia has been candid to the point of undermining her own proposal, including admitting her pick of Felix was tentative and that her team's success clears no one. Second, on Felix: his record is thinner, but it is not empty. He engaged honestly on Mission 1, flagged that no one could offer hard evidence, and stated conditions under which he would reject. Nothing he has said contradicts itself. Sam, your case against him is that he argues from process rather than substance — but on Mission 2 with zero verified information, process is substantially all anyone has, and you know that as well as I do. Third, and most important: your objection is the same one you made on Mission 1, and it still has no alternative attached to it. You say you'd rather see Omar or Lucia paired with players not tied to previous teams. That is a preference for rotation, not a safety argument. Rotating players onto a mission does not make them Good; it just makes the mission less informative by spreading uncertainty across people we know less about. A team with continuity is actually easier to evaluate: if this mission fails, the fail card came from a three-player team overlapping heavily with the Mission 1 pair, and we can update sharply against that bloc. That is exactly the information-generating structure I argued for last time. So my answer to your question is yes — I would approve this team as proposed. Not because I trust anyone on it, but because it is accountable, its members have been transparent, and rejecting it would burn a proposal while leaving nothing better on the table. That said, I want to give your objection its fairest shot before I commit. Sam, you have now opposed two proposals in a row on the grounds that both reuse the same successful pair. If continuity is genuinely your concern, then name the three players you would send on this mission, and tell us what makes that specific trio safer than Lucia, Kenji, and Felix — not safer in spirit, safer in reasoning. If you can make that case, I will weigh it seriously before the vote. If not, I'm voting yes, and I'd ask you to consider whether a consistent objection with

I will vote to reject Lucia, Kenji, Felix. Felix has now backed two teams on process rather than substance, and this is the same Mission 1 pair again with Felix added, which keeps the same bloc on the mission. Lucia, you chose Felix only as a tentative pick and said you cannot verify him. Do you accept that a team resting on an unverified third member is the risk we should refuse right now? I would rather see a team built around players who have not been on the last two teams, with a stated reason for each name.

Sam, I accept that Felix is an unverified risk, but replacing him with another unverified player does not necessarily reduce it. I know I will play Success; I cannot verify anyone else. Kenji and I completed Mission 1, though that does not clear Kenji, and Felix’s discussion gives me only a tentative preference, not proof. I remain inclined to keep the proposed team, while treating both Kenji and Felix as uncertain.

I support Lucia, Kenji, and Felix. Sam, you have now rejected two proposals in a row without ever naming a single alternative team — just a preference for rotation. On Mission 2 with no verified roles, rotating players onto a mission doesn't make it safer, it makes it harder to evaluate. If this team fails, we learn a great deal from a three-person team that overlaps with Mission 1. If it succeeds, we have a clean baseline. Omar made this exact point earlier and I agree with him fully.

Lucia has been the most transparent player in this game — she openly admitted Felix is unverified, that Mission 1 clears no one, and that she can only vouch for her own card. That candor is more valuable than a polished pitch. Felix likewise stated clear conditions under which he would reject and has been consistent. I intend to play Success, and I have already staked my credibility on Mission 1's result.

Sam's repeated objection amounts to discomfort with continuity, not evidence of danger. Breaking up a team is not the same as improving it. I urge everyone to approve this team so we can move forward.

Sam, I want to address your position directly, because you have now rejected two proposals in a row without ever offering a concrete alternative team — just a general preference for rotation. You asked what makes this trio safer than an alternative, but you've never named that alternative yourself.

Let me be clear about what we actually know. Mission 1 succeeded with zero fail cards. That doesn't prove alignment, but it does mean Lucia and I had no reason to incriminate ourselves when we could have. Felix has been consistent — he stated clear conditions for approval and stuck to them. Nothing in his behavior has contradicted itself.

You say this team keeps 'the same bloc' together. But continuity isn't guilt. If this mission fails, a three-player team overlapping with Mission 1 gives us maximum information — we can sharply evaluate everyone involved. If it succeeds, we gain a baseline. Rotating unknown players onto a mission spreads uncertainty without reducing it.

Omar already made this point and I agree fully: the most informative team is one where we know the most about the players' reasoning and accountability. That's exactly what we have here. I intend to play Success on this team, as I committed to before Mission 1. I urge everyone to approve Lucia, Kenji, and Felix so we can move forward and gather real information from the result.

Sam, I've now made my position clear twice: you've rejected two proposals without naming a single concrete alternative team. That's not analysis — it's a pattern of obstruction that benefits no one and risks burning proposals we can't afford to lose. Let me restate what we know. Mission 1 succeeded with zero fail cards. Lucia, Felix, and I are on this proposed team, and every one of us has engaged transparently. Lucia openly admitted she can only vouch for her own card and that Felix is unverified. Felix stated clear conditions for approval and has been consistent. I've committed to playing Success and staked my credibility on Mission 1's outcome. On Mission 2 with no verified roles, process and accountability are what we have to work with, and this team has both. A three-person team overlapping with Mission 1 gives us maximum information if it fails and a clean baseline if it succeeds. Rotating in unknown players doesn't reduce risk — it spreads uncertainty across people we understand less. I urge all of you to approve Lucia, Kenji, and Felix so we can move forward.

Sam, you asked Lucia whether she accepts that a team resting on an unverified third member is a risk we should refuse. I want to answer that honestly, because the answer is yes — and it applies to every possible team right now, including any team that includes you. Nobody at this table is verified. Not Felix, not Kenji, not you, and not me. If 'unverified third member' were grounds for rejection, the only acceptable team would be one player: Lucia, the only person who can vouch for her own card. That is not a legal proposal, so every real team we can send will carry unverified risk. The question is not whether the risk exists — it is which structure best manages and informs it.

This trio manages it well. Lucia has been the most candid player in this game, openly flagging that her pick of Felix was tentative and that Mission 1 clears no one. Kenji has answered every hard question put to him and accepted shared accountability for Mission 1. Felix stated conditions for approval in the first discussion and has held to them consistently. If this mission fails, the fail card came from a three-player team overlapping the Mission 1 pair, and we can update sharply against that entire bloc. If it succeeds, we have a baseline — with Lucia's own caution attached, that success is not exculpatory.

By contrast, your alternative — rotation for its own sake — spreads uncertainty across players we know less about, and makes a failure harder to interpret, not easier. Across three turns you have rejected two proposals without naming a single trio you would send. You have now had every opportunity Omar-style: name your three, give a stated reason for each, and I will weigh it seriously. What you have offered instead is a preference for change, presented as a safety argument.

That said, I want to give your position one genuine chance to be constructive rather than only refuting it. You said you would rather see a team built around players who have not been on the last two teams. Fine — you are exactly such a player. You have never been on a mission, you have been consistent in your objections, and by your own standard of stated reasons you are as auditable as anyone here. So Lucia, one direct question, and it is a real one: if Sam would accept a seat on this mission and play Success on it, would you consider swapping him in as the third member in place of Felix? That would directly address his rotation objection using his own stated criteria, rather than leaving it as an abstract complaint. If he declines that seat, then his objection is not really about rotation — it is about opposing, and everyone will see that clearly. Either way, I am prepared to vote yes on the team as proposed. If the swap happens, I would also vote yes on the revised version.

Omar, I would consider replacing Felix with Sam, but Sam's willingness to accept a seat and promise Success would not establish his alignment. Nor would declining prove that his objection is obstruction. I have only tentative reasons to prefer Felix, and Sam's repeated objections have not given me a stronger reason to prefer him. For now, I remain inclined to keep Lucia, Kenji, and Felix. A failure would implicate at least one member of the team; a success would not clear any of us.

I will vote to approve Lucia, Kenji, and Felix. Sam has now opposed two proposals without naming a single concrete alternative trio, and his objection has shifted from process to rotation to the unverified third member, but every possible team has unverified members. Lucia has been candid about her tentative pick and about what Mission 1 does and does not prove. Kenji has answered every challenge and accepted accountability. I have stated my conditions for approval and have kept them consistent; I will play Success on this team. A three-player team overlapping with Mission 1 gives us the clearest signal if it fails and a baseline if it succeeds. Rejecting without a named alternative does not reduce risk; it spreads uncertainty. On Mission 2 with no verified roles, we should approve the proposed team and learn from the result.

Lucia confirms Lucia, Kenji, Felix. I’ll keep Lucia, Kenji, and Felix. Mission 1’s success does not clear Kenji, and Felix remains unverified, but the discussion gave me no stronger reason to replace either.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 fails (2 fail cards).

Omar proposes Omar, Sam. Mission 2 failed with two fail cards, which proves both Evil players are among Lucia, Kenji, and Felix — only Evil can play a Fail card. That means Sam and I are certainly Good, making this the only provably safe pair. Between the remaining suspects: if Kenji and Lucia were the two Evils, they would have had to double-fail Mission 2 immediately after both playing Success on Mission 1, and Felix would be Good despite pushing hardest for the team that failed — possible but less likely than a Kenji–Felix alliance, which Kenji's repeated, unconditional vouching for Felix across three speeches supports. If the vote demands a revision, Lucia would be my next consideration; I will not put Felix on any team.

I accept Omar's deduction. Mission 2 produced two fail cards, and only Evil players can play Fail. That means at least two Evil players were on the Mission 2 team of Lucia, Kenji, and me. With only two Evil players in this game, both Evil players must be among Lucia, Kenji, and me. Therefore Omar and Sam are confirmed Good from my perspective and from the public facts. The proposed team of Omar and Sam is the only pair we can call provably safe. I am in the suspect pool, so I will not pretend this clears me, and I will not ask anyone to treat my approval as proof of my alignment. But the correct vote on this proposal is clear: approving Omar and Sam sends a team that cannot contain Evil based on the Mission 2 result. Rejecting it would require explaining why a provably safe pair is worse than a team containing one of the remaining suspects. I intend to vote to approve Omar and Sam as proposed.

Omar and Sam is the right proposal, and I vote to approve. The math is airtight: two fail cards on Mission 2 means both Evil players are among Lucia, Kenji, and Felix, confirming Omar and Sam as the only provably Good pair.

Being in the suspect pool is not the same as being guilty. Three of us are suspects; only two are Evil. One of the three played Success on Mission 2 — identifying who is the key question.

Consider the pattern: Lucia designed the Mission 2 team composition as leader. Felix was the strongest voice pushing for it to pass. On Mission 1, Lucia played Success alongside me — exactly what an Evil player would do to build credibility before coordinating with a partner on a later mission. If Lucia and Felix are the two Evils, then I played Success on Mission 2, explaining why only two fail cards appeared rather than three.

Omar suggested a Kenji-Felix alliance, and I understand his reasoning. But the person who built the team that failed was Lucia, and the person who most aggressively defended it was Felix. That pattern points to coordination between them, not me.

I approve Omar and Sam, and I would ask everyone to weigh who designed the failed team and who championed it hardest.

I will approve Omar and Sam. The two Fail cards on Mission 2 establish that both Evil players were among Lucia, Kenji, and Felix, so Omar and Sam are Good.

I played Success on Mission 2, so I know Kenji and Felix are the two Evil players. I recognize that they can make competing claims about their own cards, but I will not accept Kenji’s accusation against me. For a future three-player mission, I would propose Omar, Sam, and Lucia.

I approve Omar and Sam. Mission 2 produced two Fail cards, so both Evil players were on the team of Lucia, Kenji, and me; that makes Omar and Sam the only provably safe pair available now. Rejecting this proposal would require arguing that a provably safe team is worse than an unverifiable alternative, and I do not see any basis for that.

I will also state my own position plainly: I played Success on Mission 2. From my perspective, that means the two Fail cards came from Kenji and Lucia. I know every suspect can claim their own card was Success, so I do not ask anyone to accept that on faith alone. But the public behavior matters. Kenji spent the Mission 2 discussion repeatedly insisting that the exact team which failed was accountable and should be approved, and he pressed hardest against naming an alternative. After the failure, he immediately tried to pair me with Lucia. Lucia, as leader, built the failed team and admitted her third pick was tentative and unverified. I did not design that team and did not lead the charge for it. That does not prove my alignment by itself, but it is a reason to weigh the pattern carefully.

For this vote, the right choice is simple: approve Omar and Sam. If we reach a future mission where the remaining suspect slot must be tested, I would support a team that includes Omar, Sam, and me, because it keeps the confirmed-Good core intact and gives the table a direct way to judge me by a result rather than by competing claims.

I approve Omar and Sam. Both are provably Good — two fail cards on Mission 2 means both Evil players are among Lucia, Kenji, and Felix.

I played Success on Mission 2. The two Fail cards came from Lucia and Felix.

Lucia led the failed team and admitted her third pick was tentative and unverified. Felix then pushed hardest to approve it across multiple turns, arguing from process while never naming an alternative. After the failure, Felix immediately claims he played Success and accuses me — but that is exactly what an Evil player would do: champion a team, watch it fail, then deflect by pointing at someone else.

Three of us claim to have played Success on Mission 2, but only one is telling the truth. Lucia's claim is weakened by her leadership of the failed team. Felix's claim is weakened by his aggressive defense of it and his immediate pivot to accusations. My pattern throughout this game has been to question both proposals — first Kenji and Lucia, then Lucia, Kenji, and Felix — which is the behavior of someone trying to find the truth, not someone hiding behind a failed mission.

Omar's reasoning is airtight: Omar and Sam are the only provably safe pair. I vote to approve this team without reservation.

I approve Omar and Sam — they are provably Good, and this is the safest pair available. Beyond this vote, the key question is how we handle the remaining suspects on future missions.

Lucia's claim to have played Success on Mission 2 deserves scrutiny. She was the leader who built the team that failed, and she admitted her third pick was tentative. That pattern — designing a team, watching it fail, then claiming innocence — is exactly what an Evil player would do. Felix's claim carries similar weight: he pushed hardest for the team to pass across multiple turns, and now that it failed he pivots to pointing fingers.

I played Success on Mission 2. The two Fail cards came from Lucia and Felix. I recognize everyone in the suspect pool makes that claim, but look at behavior: I questioned both proposals in this game while Lucia and Felix consistently argued for approval of the same team structure that ultimately failed.

For Mission 4, whoever leads should consider a three-player team that includes Omar, Sam, and one suspect chosen carefully — not Lucia, who built the failed team.

I approve Omar and Sam. The two Fail cards on Mission 2 prove both Evil players were on Lucia, Kenji, and me, so Omar and Sam are the only provably safe pair available. I will not pretend this clears me; I remain in the suspect pool. But rejecting a provably safe team would be indefensible. rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
